idiom_name: @functools.cache keyed factory returning the canonical instance
implementation_notes: The shortest Python multiton is a module-level factory decorated with functools.cache (3.9+; lru_cache(maxsize=None) before that): the first call for a key constructs the object, every later call returns that same object, and the cache is the registry - the docs describe cache as a thin wrapper around a dictionary lookup on the arguments. Keys must be hashable, maxsize must be None (a bounded lru_cache may evict, and eviction silently breaks instance identity), and the docs note the wrapped function can still run more than once if another thread calls before the first result is cached.
pitfalls: Unhashable arguments (list, dict, set) raise TypeError at call time - normalise to tuple or frozenset, and remember different argument spellings produce different entries.
Never use lru_cache with a finite maxsize for identity-bearing instances: an evicted entry means the next call creates a second pool while the first is still in use.
Construction may run twice under a race (documented); when exactly-once construction matters, guard the factory with a lock or use a class registry.

variants.name: Module-level registry dict (or class __new__ registry)
variants.idiom_name: module dict + threading.Lock, or a class whose __new__ returns the per-key instance
variants.implementation_notes: The hand-rolled form: a module-level dict keyed by the identity key, a threading.Lock held across find-or-create, and a factory function - or a class whose __new__ returns the cached instance per key. The data model notes that when __new__ returns an existing instance, __init__ is invoked again on it, so the constructor must be idempotent; choose this form when the registry must expose reset/close_all, when the key has identity semantics rather than a hashable value, or when entries must be evictable.
pitfalls: __new__ returning a cached instance makes __init__ run again on it, so side-effecting constructors re-initialise the shared object unless guarded.
The GIL does not make check-then-set atomic: without the lock two threads can both construct, and the discarded pool's sockets stay open.
The dict keeps every instance alive for the process; with per-request keys it grows without bound, so a registry is not a substitute for a cache with eviction.
